terms.gloss: Ostap Bender, the young con man and protagonist; here posing as 'Voldemar/Vladimir Ippolitovich'
terms.why_hard: one fixed transliteration must serve the whole book; don't localize or vary the spelling

proposed.ja: オスタップ・ベンデル

terms.gloss: Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov, ex-marshal of the nobility whose family furniture is being traced
terms.why_hard: long patronymic name; must match every other page and not be shortened inconsistently

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇·沃罗比亚尼诺夫
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ・ヴォロビヤニノフ

terms.gloss: the old archivist keeping a private duplicate of the furniture-requisition records
terms.why_hard: surname echoes 'peddler'; keep as a name, transliterate consistently

terms.gloss: the bashful embezzler who runs the 2nd Home of Sobes; recurs elsewhere
terms.why_hard: nickname form; fix one spelling so the cross-reference to his home lands

terms.gloss: Comrade Gritsatsuev, war invalid granted one chair; links to the widow Gritsatsueva later
terms.why_hard: same stem as a later character; keep the shared surname visible across languages

proposed.ja: グリツァツーエフ同志

terms.gloss: old-fashioned word for an archives keeper; a pre-revolutionary chancery flavour
terms.why_hard: not the neutral 'archivist'; carries a fussy, bygone-clerk tone

terms.gloss: comic Soviet compound: a meat-chilling and slaughtering works, Ostap's fake trade
terms.why_hard: an absurd bureaucratic portmanteau; render as a mouthful, not a smooth 'butcher shop'

terms.gloss: merchant of the first guild, top tier of the pre-revolutionary merchant estate
terms.why_hard: a defunct legal rank, not just 'rich merchant'; needs a rendering that reads as a formal grade

terms.gloss: municipal communal-services department that officially owns the requisitioned furniture
terms.why_hard: clipped Soviet acronym; give a transparent calque, keep it fixed

proposed.ja: 公共事業部（コムンホーズ）

terms.gloss: the 2nd Home run by Sobes (the social-welfare office); an old-people's home, Alkhen's post
terms.why_hard: 'собес' is an acronym for the welfare dept; 'дом' here means a residential home, not a house

proposed.zh: 社会保障局第二养老院
proposed.ja: 社会保障局第二ホーム

terms.gloss: city military commissariat, the local draft/military-affairs office
terms.why_hard: acronym; a reader needs the expanded sense, not four opaque letters

terms.gloss: Stargorod provincial food-supply committee; a dense stack of clipped words
terms.why_hard: extreme portmanteau; the comedy is in its unwieldiness, so keep it recognizably a mouthful

proposed.zh: 斯塔尔哥罗德省粮食委员会
proposed.ja: スタルゴロド県食糧委員会

terms.gloss: People's Commissariat of Foreign Trade
terms.why_hard: standard Narkom- acronym; use the established English calque and match it book-wide

terms.gloss: Main Tea Administration, the state tea monopoly's head office
terms.why_hard: Glav- 'main administration' acronym; the joke is a whole bureau just for tea

terms.gloss: People's Commissariat of Education/Enlightenment, which took the ten chairs to a Moscow museum
terms.why_hard: well-known acronym; keep the standard rendering consistent with other volumes

terms.gloss: the housing department, and 'zavzhilotdelom' its head, who signed off a chair
terms.why_hard: acronymic office plus an acronymic job title; both need transparent renderings

proposed.en: housing dept. / head of the housing dept.
proposed.zh: 住房处 / 住房处主任

terms.gloss: Hero of Labour, an actual Soviet honorific; Ostap uses it as mock flattery
terms.why_hard: a real title, not a generic compliment; render as the recognizable award

terms.term: Ближе к телу, как говорит Мопассан
terms.gloss: Ostap's garble of 'ближе к делу' (get to the point) into 'closer to the body', falsely credited to Maupassant
terms.why_hard: the joke is the malaprop + misattribution; a literal 'let's get to business' kills it

proposed.en: Closer to the body, as Maupassant says (for 'closer to the point')
proposed.zh: 还是贴身点好，正如莫泊桑所说（把“说正题”误成“贴身”）
proposed.ja: もっと体に近く、モーパッサン曰く（「本題に入る」の言い間違い）

terms.gloss: 'oats are dear nowadays', a cabman's stock excuse for a high fare; Ostap haggles by treating the price as one
terms.why_hard: reads as a non sequitur unless the cabby-overcharging idiom carries over

proposed.en: Oats are dear these days, are they?
proposed.ja: 近ごろ燕麦が高いものでね

terms.gloss: echo of Pushkin's 'Exegi monumentum' ('a monument not made by hands'); mock-solemn praise
terms.why_hard: a famous quotation; render so a reader hears the lofty-verse register being spoofed

proposed.en: raise you a monument not made by hands
proposed.zh: 该给您立一座非人手所造的丰碑
proposed.ja: 人の手によらぬ記念碑を建てて差し上げたい

terms.gloss: Ostap's pet malapropism, used to mean 'sheer genius / brilliant'
terms.why_hard: not English 'congenial'; keep the showy misused word rather than a plain 'brilliant'

proposed.en: It's congenial! (Ostap-speak for 'a stroke of genius')
proposed.zh: 太天才了！（奥斯塔普爱用的误词）
proposed.ja: 実に天才的だ！（オスタップの誤用癖）

terms.gloss: made by the master Gambs, the famed St. Petersburg furniture firm; the twelve chairs are Gambs chairs
terms.why_hard: central to the whole plot; keep 'Gambs' as the maker's name, don't generic-ize to 'fine craftsmanship'

proposed.en: the work of the master Gambs

conventions: Soviet acronym-institutions (Наркомпрос, Главчай, собес, Коммунхоз, Старпродкомгуб…): render as a transparent calque the reader parses at sight (e.g. 'People's Commissariat of Education', 'Main Tea Administration'), never a bare transliteration, and bind one rendering per institution across the whole book.
Character names: fix one transliteration per language and reuse it everywhere; do not translate meaningful-sounding surnames (Vorobyaninov, Korobeinikov).

Ostap's malapropisms and misquotations (конгениально, 'ближе к телу, как говорит Мопассан', 'памятник нерукотворный') keep the deadpan garble in the target text rather than being silently corrected; add a translator's note only when the pun would otherwise vanish.

meta.summary: object with keys [rank, terms, chapter_titles, conventions, page_types]

terms.gloss: Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov, ex-marshal of the nobility, one of the two treasure-hunters
terms.why_hard: addressed by name+patronymic and by surname Воробьянинов; both must stay one consistent identity

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇（沃罗比亚尼诺夫）
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ（ヴォロビヤニノフ）

terms.gloss: parish priest of the Frol-and-Lavr church, Vorobyaninov's rival for the chair
terms.why_hard: also called отец Федор, батюшка, святой отец, духовная особа — all one man, all must read as clergy

proposed.zh: 费奥多尔神父（沃斯特里科夫）
proposed.ja: フョードル神父（ヴォストリコフ）

terms.term: технический директор и главный руководитель концессии
terms.gloss: Ostap Bender's mock-corporate self-title as head of the treasure hunt
terms.why_hard: Остап is named only obliquely here; the pompous title is a running joke and must sound bureaucratic-grand

proposed.en: technical director and chief manager of the concession (Ostap)
proposed.zh: 特许公司技术总监兼总经理（奥斯塔普）
proposed.ja: コンセッションの技術部長兼総支配人（オスタップ）

terms.gloss: marshal of the nobility, Vorobyaninov's pre-revolutionary elected office
terms.why_hard: a tsarist estate rank, not a generic 'leader'; carries his fallen social status

terms.gloss: a chair from the famous St. Petersburg furniture firm of H. D. Gambs; the whole plot hinges on the set
terms.why_hard: 'Gambs/Hambs' is a proper maker's name, not an adjective; signals bourgeois pedigree

terms.gloss: a Soviet mill-construction trust; here a passing lorry stamped with the acronym
terms.why_hard: NEP-era portmanteau acronym (Мельничное строительство); should look like a Soviet trust name

proposed.zh: 面粉厂建设托拉斯（梅尔斯特罗伊）
proposed.ja: メリストロイ（製粉建設トラスト）

terms.gloss: the newspaper Izvestia, cried in a vendor's mangled non-Russian accent (гайзета «Звестие»)
terms.why_hard: the point is the mispronunciation of a real paper; a clean 'Izvestia' loses the joke

proposed.zh: 莫斯科报《兹韦斯》（即《消息报》）
proposed.ja: モスクワの新聞『ズヴェスチヤ』（イズヴェスチヤ）

terms.gloss: a popular Soviet satirical magazine of the 1920s (The Laugher)
terms.why_hard: a real period title; keep it as a name, gloss the meaning

proposed.ja: 雑誌『スメハーチ（笑い屋）』

terms.gloss: an illustrated literary weekly of the 1920s (Red Cornfield)
terms.why_hard: real period title; 'нива' is a poetic 'cornfield/tilth', not literal

proposed.ja: 『赤い畑（クラスナヤ・ニーヴァ）』

terms.gloss: a Soviet militia policeman
terms.why_hard: not 'militiaman' in the paramilitary sense; it is the ordinary Soviet police

terms.gloss: the Krakowiak, a lively Polish folk dance; here the simile for his dodging footwork
terms.why_hard: a named dance, not a generic jig; keep the specific name

proposed.ja: クラコヴィヤク（ポーランド舞踊）

terms.gloss: the church of Saints Florus and Laurus, where Father Fyodor serves
terms.why_hard: 'Фрол и Лавр' are the Russian forms of two saints; keep as a church dedication

proposed.en: the church of Frol and Lavr (Sts. Florus and Laurus)
proposed.ja: フロルとラヴル（聖フロルスと聖ラウルス）教会

terms.gloss: affectionate/respectful form of address to an Orthodox priest
terms.why_hard: warm 'father', not 'daddy'; register shifts from mocking to sincere and must read as clergy address

terms.gloss: Soviet power/the Soviet authorities as the nationalizing agent
terms.why_hard: a fixed political term ('Soviet power'), not just 'the government'

terms.gloss: 'the power of the workers and peasants', a stock revolutionary formula
terms.why_hard: a slogan cadence (paired with 'властью трудящихся'); keep the formulaic ring

proposed.en: by the power of the workers and peasants
proposed.ja: 労働者と農民の権力によって

terms.gloss: nationalized property — the legal status Father Fyodor claims for the chair
terms.why_hard: a Soviet legal term; the comic force is the priest wielding Bolshevik jargon

terms.gloss: a member of the Communist Party
terms.why_hard: 'party' = the Party; a priest being 'партийный' is the punchline, so keep it a Party-membership word

terms.gloss: the housing department of the local soviet
terms.why_hard: another NEP acronym (жилищный отдел); should read as a Soviet office

terms.gloss: an almshouse/poorhouse; the chair was bought there for three roubles
terms.why_hard: pre-revolutionary charity institution, distinct from a modern care home

terms.gloss: a NEP-era shimmy song Ostap hums ('camels used to do it, the batakudy danced it')
terms.why_hard: the Shimmy fad + nonsense-exotic 'ба-та-ку-ды'; keep the song's silly period flavour, don't over-explain

terms.gloss: a street renamed for the 1912 Lena Goldfields massacre
terms.why_hard: 'Ленские события' is the euphemism for the Lena shootings; a literal 'Lena Events St.' hides the reference

terms.gloss: a swindler/con man — Vorobyaninov's insult to the priest
terms.why_hard: swindler with a whiff of confidence-trickster, not merely 'crook'

conventions: Keep вы between the two brawlers: they trade blows while addressing each other with formal 'вы' and titles (святой отец, уважаемый) — the comedy is the courtesy, so never flatten to casual English 'you'.
Render dialogue with em-dash openers as in the source and preserve the clipped stichomythia ('— А чье же? — Не ваше.') without adding speech tags.
In Japanese distinguish clergy honorifics (神父さま for батюшка's warm register vs 聖なる神父 for the mock-solemn 'святой отец') and keep the narrator's deadpan mock-solemn asides in plain 常体.

conventions: Dialogue set off by an em dash in Russian is rendered with the target language's own dialogue punctuation: quotation marks for en, 「」 for ja, and 引号/破折号 consistently for zh; the mock-solemn narratorial asides stay in plain narrative voice.

Given-name+patronymic address (Виктор Михайлович, Елена Станиславовна, Ипполит Матвеевич) is transliterated in full and kept identical everywhere; ja uses katakana with ・ separators, and no target-language honorific is substituted for the patronymic.

Soviet/NEP clipped office-names (жилтоварищество, коммунхоз, жилотдел, Быстроупак) and mock-officialese (при наличии отсутствия) keep their bureaucratic, comically invented flavor rather than being normalized to modern generic terms.

conventions: Names: transliterate consistently and keep the full first-name + patronymic + surname system (Ипполит Матвеевич Воробьянинов) intact; link each character's diminutives (Паша/Пашка) to one canonical spelling rather than domesticating.

terms.why_hard: there is no church clergy here; the reader must grasp this is the state office that replaced parish records

terms.gloss: cheap violet alizarin copying-ink, the standard smell of a 1920s Soviet office
terms.why_hard: a period-specific sensory detail; must read as bureaucratic drabness, not as an exotic chemical

terms.gloss: spring-clip document folder 'No. 2', prop of the fussy clerk
terms.why_hard: recurs a second time on the page; keep the same office-supply term both times

terms.gloss: the bridegroom's blurted single word for 'to be joined [in wedlock]', an old bookish/ecclesiastical verb
terms.why_hard: must sound stiff and half-remembered, prompting Vorobyaninov's deadpan 'Birth? Death?'

terms.gloss: the 'Plough and Hammer' co-operative (a joke twist on hammer-and-sickle), where a rooster crows at noon
terms.why_hard: the name parodies Soviet emblems; the pun is lost if rendered as a plain shop name

terms.gloss: 'Comrade Gubernsky Street', a street renamed for a functionary whose name puns on губерния (province)
terms.why_hard: reads as an ordinary surname unless the province pun and the mania for renaming streets come through

proposed.ja: グベルンスキー同志通り

terms.gloss: the district (uyezd) executive committee's motorcar, state plate No. 1 — the only official car in town
terms.why_hard: 'uispolkom' is an opaque Soviet acronym; the joke is that state car No. 1 is a wheezing wreck

proposed.en: the district-soviet's car, State Plate No. 1
proposed.zh: 县执委会的汽车，公牌1号
proposed.ja: 郡執行委員会の車、公用一号車

terms.gloss: Staropanskaya ('Old-Gentry') Square, the town's central square
terms.why_hard: the name still carries the pre-revolutionary 'pan/gentry' flavour the new regime hasn't erased

proposed.ja: スタロパンスカヤ広場

terms.gloss: 'staff reduction', the layoffs the clerks dread and gossip about
terms.why_hard: period bureaucratic phrase; must read as the era's job-anxiety idiom, not generic 'cuts'

terms.gloss: 'Welcome' — the name of a now-defunct rival undertaker Bezenchuk recalls nostalgically
terms.why_hard: a shop name, not a greeting; the humour is a funeral firm called 'Welcome'

proposed.ja: 葬儀店「いらっしゃいませ」

terms.gloss: glacé/silver brocade used to line and cover coffins; a mark of quality in the coffin trade
terms.why_hard: an obsolete fabric term specific to undertaking; must not be flattened to plain 'cloth'

terms.gloss: Bezenchuk's untranslatable folksy oath, roughly 'blast the thing', repeated as a verbal tic
terms.why_hard: recurs whenever Bezenchuk speaks; needs one fixed, rustic, mildly profane phrase applied verbatim book-wide

terms.gloss: Bezenchuk's boast that his coffin is 'a little cucumber' — i.e. a prime, hand-picked specimen
terms.why_hard: a Russian food metaphor for excellence; literal 'cucumber' would baffle the reader

proposed.en: "a coffin like a peach — top-grade, deluxe"
proposed.zh: “这棺材，顶呱呱，精挑细选的上等货”
proposed.ja: 「この棺は極上でさ、選りすぐりの逸品で」

terms.term: лучи солнца лежали на плечах, как эполеты
terms.gloss: sunbeams lie on Vorobyaninov's shoulders 'like epaulettes', summoning his officer/noble past (he once wore a corset)
terms.why_hard: the epaulettes/corset cues signal his pre-revolutionary rank; drop them and his mock-grandeur is lost

proposed.en: lay on his shoulders like epaulettes
proposed.zh: 像肩章一样搭在他肩上
proposed.ja: 肩章のように肩に載っていた

terms.gloss: Vorobyaninov's biconcave-lensed pince-nez, a recurring emblem of his fading gentility
terms.why_hard: an iconic recurring object; keep one term, not alternating 'glasses/spectacles'

conventions: Bezenchuk's oath «туды её в качель» and his coffin-jargon ('a coffin like a cucumber', глазет) each get ONE fixed rendering reused verbatim wherever he speaks, since his voice recurs through all the coffin scenes.

Keep Vorobyaninov's ex-noble, mock-solemn register elevated and faintly archaic in all three languages (epaulettes, corset, 'as they used to say'); in Japanese use keigo for his public wedding speeches against plain forms for the dry narrator.
ты/вы: Vorobyaninov addresses Bezenchuk with condescending ты — mark the status gap (plain/blunt forms in ja; 你 plus deferential undertaker's speech in zh).

terms.gloss: The young con man, the novel's 'grand schemer' hero.
terms.why_hard: Recurring name; transliteration must be fixed once and match the chapter title 'Великий комбинатор'.

proposed.ja: オスタップ・ベンデル

terms.gloss: Former marshal of the nobility, the other treasure-hunter.
terms.why_hard: Full name+patronymic here but later shortened (Kisa/Vorobyaninov); forms must be tracked consistently.

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇·沃罗比亚尼诺夫
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ・ヴォロビヤニノフ

terms.gloss: The old servant now working as the building's dvornik.
terms.why_hard: Simple name, but must be fixed since he recurs.

terms.gloss: Yard-keeper: caretaker, doorman and watchman with quasi-police duties, not merely a cleaner.
terms.why_hard: 'Janitor' loses the surveillance/watchman role central to the period; a recurring role word.

terms.gloss: The dvornik's lodge, where the whole scene plays out.
terms.why_hard: Must match the chosen rendering of 'дворник'; not a generic room.

terms.gloss: Pre-revolutionary form of address 'master/gentleman' used by a servant.
terms.why_hard: Class-laden deference; a flat 'sir' loses Tikhon's obsolete servility. Recurs.

terms.gloss: Former marshal of the nobility — an elected pre-1917 provincial office.
terms.why_hard: 'Leader/chief' is wrong; it is a specific defunct rank that defines Vorobyaninov.

terms.gloss: Casual slang for 'bumped off / shot' (summary execution).
terms.why_hard: Blackly comic euphemism for execution; a neutral 'killed' loses the offhand register.

terms.gloss: Contemptuous collective for soldiers, 'the soldier rabble'.
terms.why_hard: The pejorative -ня suffix must survive; plain 'soldiers' is neutral and wrong.

terms.gloss: State Political Directorate, the political police (successor to the Cheka).
terms.why_hard: Acronym for a specific 1920s secret-police body; recurs and drives the threat gags.

proposed.zh: 国家政治保卫局（格伯乌）
proposed.ja: ゲーペーウー（国家政治保安部）

terms.gloss: White émigré — someone who fled Soviet Russia after 1917.
terms.why_hard: Not 'immigrant/migrant'; the joke is the accusation of being a returned White émigré.

terms.gloss: A twist on the popular romance 'Белой акации гроздья душистые' ('fragrant clusters of white acacia'), remade into 'flowers of emigration'.
terms.why_hard: Pure song allusion; without a note the reader misses that Ostap is quoting-and-mangling a well-known romance.

proposed.en: 'White acacia, flowers of emigration…' (parodying the romance 'Fragrant clusters of white acacia')
proposed.zh: “白洋槐，流亡之花……”（戏仿名曲《芬芳的白洋槐花串》）
proposed.ja: 「白いアカシア、亡命の花よ…」（名歌《香る白アカシアの房》のもじり）

terms.gloss: A 'pre-war' sparkle — i.e. pre-1914 / pre-revolutionary, seen through his pince-nez.
terms.why_hard: 'War' here means WWI, not WWII; the dating carries the whole nostalgic joke.

proposed.ja: 戦前（第一次大戦前）の輝き

terms.gloss: Colloquial name for a ten-kopeck coin.
terms.why_hard: A specific small coin, not just 'a dime/a few coppers'; recurs as a unit of tiny sums.

terms.gloss: DOPR — 'house of forced labour', a 1920s corrective-detention institution.
terms.why_hard: Period-specific penal acronym; 'jail/prison' erases the era-specific institution.

terms.gloss: A parcel of food/goods brought to a prisoner.
terms.why_hard: Not 'transmission/broadcast'; the specific prison-parcel sense drives the anecdote's punchline.

terms.gloss: Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic (the state Vorobyaninov claims citizenship of).
terms.why_hard: A specific state acronym; must be rendered consistently, not conflated with USSR.

proposed.zh: 俄罗斯苏维埃联邦社会主义共和国
proposed.ja: ロシア・ソビエト連邦社会主義共和国

terms.gloss: An illegal currency speculator / black-market money dealer.
terms.why_hard: Criminal-FX slang of the NEP years; 'financier' or 'trader' misses the illegality.

proposed.ja: 闇両替屋（通貨ブローカー）

terms.gloss: Ostap's grandiose pet word, roughly 'brilliant / perfectly matched'.
terms.why_hard: Not English 'congenial'; a comic high-flown Ostapism whose inflated register must show.

terms.gloss: The unnamed provincial 'town of N', a Gogolian convention for Any Town.
terms.why_hard: A literary device, not a real toponym; keep the blank-name form rather than inventing a city.

terms.gloss: The diamonds sewn into a chair — the novel's central prize.
terms.why_hard: The book-long macguffin; one word must be fixed ('diamonds' vs 'jewels/brilliants').

terms.gloss: Ostap's tan/orange button-boots, part of his recurring costume.
terms.why_hard: 'Orange' color and 'штиблеты' (buttoned ankle-boots) both signal his dandy poverty; recurs.

conventions: ты/вы and rank: render the ты/вы split and master–servant deference through target register — zh 您/你, ja plain form vs. です・ます plus 旦那さま-type honorifics — because Tikhon's servility and Ostap's mock-formality are the comic engine.
Dialogue dashes: keep the Russian em-dash opening each speech line in en; in zh and ja use the native convention consistently (zh 引号/破折号, ja 「」) rather than mixing.

Proper names: transliterate all names consistently and keep full name + patronymic on formal mentions, adopting the established short forms (Kisa, Vorobyaninov, Bender) as the text introduces them; do not localize.

terms.gloss: The wife of an Orthodox priest (Fyodor's wife, Katerina Aleksandrovna)
terms.why_hard: A single lexicalized word for 'priest's wife'; must not be flattened to a bare 'wife' or mistranslated as a nun

terms.gloss: Affectionate address for a priest's wife (and how Fyodor addresses her)
terms.why_hard: Warm clerical address, not literally 'little mother'; needs a fixed familiar-respectful rendering distinct from попадья

terms.gloss: The Renovationists, the Soviet-backed reformist schism within the Orthodox Church of the 1920s
terms.why_hard: Not generic 'reformers'; a specific pro-Soviet church faction (married, modernizing clergy) that carries the joke

terms.gloss: Records clerk of the military commissariat (local conscription/registration office)
terms.why_hard: военкомат is a specific Soviet institution, not a generic 'army office'; the petty rank is part of the satire

terms.gloss: Head of the municipal-improvement subdepartment (city amenities/public works)
terms.why_hard: Mock-bureaucratic title whose comedy is its inflated length; render the full unwieldy chain, not just 'official'

terms.gloss: A triumphal arch dating from the reign of Empress Elizabeth (Petrovna), mid-18th century

proposed.zh: 伊丽莎白女皇时代的凯旋门
proposed.ja: エリザヴェータ女帝時代の凱旋門

terms.gloss: A consumer cooperative store named 'Plough and Hammer'
terms.why_hard: Parody of Soviet 'hammer and sickle' branding; the name should be translated, not transliterated, to land the gag

terms.gloss: Stocktaking / inventory audit, for which the shop was closed three weeks
terms.why_hard: Specific retail-accounting term; not 're-registration'; the absurd length of the closure is the point

terms.gloss: Period word for a cinema / picture-house (the 'illusion')
terms.why_hard: 1920s term for a movie theater; a modern 'cinema' loses the dated flavor the wife's jab relies on

terms.gloss: 'The Sinner's Mirror', a well-known didactic Russian folk print (lubok) on earthly vanity; also the chapter's title
terms.why_hard: A named traditional lubok, not a literal mirror; the archaic 'зерцало' register must be preserved

terms.gloss: A cheap Russian popular woodblock/copper print with captions, a folk-art genre
terms.why_hard: Genre term with no exact English word; 'poster' or 'cartoon' misleads; often needs a gloss on first use

terms.gloss: Church Slavonic ligature lettering, the ornate old ecclesiastical script the captions are set in
terms.why_hard: Names a specific archaic script style, not just 'Slavic writing'; signals the print's pious antiquity

proposed.ja: 教会スラヴ語の組文字

terms.term: Сим молитву деет, Хам пшеницу сеет, Яфет власть имеет. Смерть всем владеет
terms.gloss: The lubok's rhymed caption: Shem prays, Ham sows wheat, Japheth rules, Death rules all
terms.why_hard: Rhyming Slavonic verse on Noah's sons; must keep the rhyme/rhythm and the Biblical names in their canonical target forms

terms.gloss: Semyon Budyonny, famed Red Army cavalry commander whose portrait decorated soldiers' trunks
terms.why_hard: Real historical figure; the mustachioed-hero portrait is a cultural in-joke a bare transliteration drops

terms.gloss: Red Army men / soldiers of the RKKA
terms.why_hard: Specific Soviet term (Red Army), not generic 'soldiers'; fixes the 1920s milieu of the tin trunk detail

terms.gloss: Twenty gold ten-rouble coins (Tsarist gold pieces, Fyodor's hidden savings)
terms.why_hard: 'десятка' = a ten-rouble coin/note; here pre-revolutionary gold coins, distinct from the paper roubles later in the scene

proposed.ja: 二十枚の十ルーブル金貨

terms.gloss: A cassock, the long outer robe of Orthodox clergy
terms.why_hard: Specific clerical garment; 'robe'/'gown' loses the priestly register that makes lifting its hem to pocket coins funny

terms.gloss: An indelible/copying pencil (writes in ink-like purple when moistened)
terms.why_hard: Not a 'chemistry pencil'; a specific period writing tool, mistranslated by literal 'chemical'

proposed.ja: インクペンシル（褒色鉗筆）

terms.gloss: 'Cheap and Tasty', the slogan opening Fyodor's home-dinner advertisement
terms.why_hard: A stock advertising slogan; should read as a snappy fixed catchphrase, not a literal two-adjective phrase

terms.gloss: A brown duck-cloth peaked cap (part of Fyodor's borrowed civilian disguise)
terms.why_hard: картуз is a specific flat visored cap, and 'утиный' is the coarse duck fabric; the comic dowdiness is easy to lose

proposed.ja: 茶色の帆布製の鳥打帽

conventions: Clerical honorifics stay fixed book-wide: 'отец Фёдор' = Father Fyodor / 费奥多尔神父 / フョードル神父; render 'матушка'/'попадья' by role (Mother / the priest's wife), never transliterate.
The couple address each other with intimate ты; render in the plain/familiar register (Japanese だ体, no です・ます) and reserve elevated politeness markers for the narrator's mock-solemn voice.
Keep the deadpan narratorial asides intact as full sentences; render Russian em-dash dialogue as em-dashes in English and as 「」 quotation marks in Chinese and Japanese, one speaking turn per line.

terms.gloss: Ostap Bender, the young con man posing here as a fire inspector.

terms.gloss: Alchen, embezzling director of the social-security old-folks' home.

proposed.zh: 阿尔亨（亚历山大·雅科夫列维奇）

proposed.zh: 萨什亨（亚历山德拉·雅科夫列夫娜）

terms.gloss: 'The heavy legacy of the tsarist regime', a stock Soviet propaganda excuse.

proposed.ja: ツァーリ体制の重い遺産

terms.gloss: 'Nicholas-era half-whiskers': side-whiskers in the style of Nicholas I's officers, here on a woman.

terms.gloss: Zubrovka: bison-grass-flavoured vodka served at the dinner.
terms.why_hard: A specific flavoured vodka; keep the name, not a generic 'vodka', since the lavish spread is the point.

proposed.ja: ズブロッカ（バイソングラス・ウォッカ）

terms.gloss: Herring forshmak, a chopped-herring dish of the Jewish/Odessa table.

proposed.ja: ニシンのフォルシュマーク

terms.gloss: A harmonium (reed organ) and its 'vox humana' stop, cited by Ostap as fake proof of good furnishing.
terms.why_hard: 'Вокс гуманум' is the Latin organ-stop name; the joke is Ostap's pedantic name-drop. Keep the Latin term intact.

proposed.ja: ハルモニウム……ヴォクス・フマーナ

terms.gloss: 'A black-earth Battistini': a rustic singer likened to the Italian baritone Mattia Battistini.
terms.why_hard: 'Черноземный' (of the black-soil peasant belt) + the real opera star Battistini is deadpan mock-grandeur; needs the singer identified.

proposed.zh: 黑土地上的巴蒂斯蒂尼
proposed.ja: 黒土のバッティスティーニ

terms.gloss: Chastushki: rhymed comic folk ditties; here bedbugs die at the sight of the tax inspector.
terms.why_hard: Must scan and rhyme as a ditty, and 'фининспектор' (finance/tax inspector) is a topical NEP figure the joke turns on.

proposed.ja: チャストゥーシカ（滑稽小唄）；税務監査官

terms.gloss: 'Municipal/communal economy', which Ostap absurdly toasts.
terms.why_hard: Bureaucratic Soviet phrase; the comedy is toasting a dry administrative concept. Keep the officialese register.

proposed.zh: 为你们的公共事业干杯！
proposed.ja: あなた方の公共事業に！

terms.gloss: 'Kefir establishment', Ostap's mocking name for the milk-diet almshouse.

conventions: Proper names: transliterate consistently and preserve the paired mock-German pet forms (Альхен/Сашхен) and the fraternal '-евич' running gag (the four Яковлевичи + Паша Эмильевич).
Soviet acronyms/institutions (Старсобес, губпожар, красный уголок, Доризул) get a transparent in-line rendering in each language; reserve a translator's note only for genuinely opaque coinages.
Keep the narrator's dry mock-solemn register; set the wall slogans in printed capitals and let clichés (наследие царского режима) read as recognizable officialese.

proposed.zh: 师母卡捷琳娜·亚历山德罗夫娜
proposed.ja: 司祭夫人カテリーナ・アレクサンドロヴナ

terms.gloss: Mock-grandiose guild-style title for a coffin-maker/undertaker.
terms.why_hard: Flattening it to plain 'undertaker' kills the pompous archaic ring that is half the joke.

terms.gloss: Church-Slavonic euphemism for dying, applied to a small, plump old woman; genteel end of the ladder.
terms.why_hard: It is one graded rung of Bezenchuk's death-classification; must stay at the most decorous register.

terms.gloss: 'gave her soul up to God'; next rung, for a larger, thinner old woman.
terms.why_hard: Must sit just below 'преставилась' in solemnity and just above the plain slang below it.

proposed.en: gave her soul up to God
proposed.ja: 神に御魂をお返しになった

terms.gloss: Literally 'played into the box'; slang death for a tall thin man like Vorobyaninov.
terms.why_hard: Mid-register slang; the coffin-'box' pun is lost if translated as a neutral 'die'.

terms.gloss: 'bade [us] live long'; the death-phrase reserved for a merchant of the former guild.
terms.why_hard: An ironic formula (announcing death by wishing long life); a literal gloss reverses the sense.

proposed.en: bade us all a long life (departed this life)

terms.gloss: Crude slang ('keeled over / stretched his legs') for a yardman or peasant.
terms.why_hard: Low-register pair for the humble dead; must read cruder than the merchant's phrase, less crude than 'дуба дал'.

proposed.en: keeled over / turned up his toes
proposed.ja: ころりと逝った / くたばった

terms.gloss: Literally 'give the oak'; the phrase for the mightiest dead — railway conductors and officials.
terms.why_hard: The joke is that the grandest people get the crudest verb; keep it blunt and keep the irony of rank.

terms.gloss: The lowest, most dismissive death-word, which Bezenchuk expects for himself as 'a small man'.
terms.why_hard: Must be the crudest and most throwaway of the set, matching his self-deprecation.

terms.gloss: Glacé brocade shot with silver/gold thread, used to trim expensive coffins.
terms.why_hard: Not 'glaze'; a specific costly funeral fabric — with 'кисти' (tassels) it marks the upgraded coffin Vorobyaninov finally orders.

terms.gloss: Fire chief (Germanic loanword); here the fire brigade sings mock-praise to 'товарищ Насосов' (Comrade Pump).
terms.why_hard: Bureaucratic loanword plus the pun name Насосов (насос='pump') carry the satire of Soviet ceremonial song.

proposed.zh: 消防队长；纳索索夫同志（“水泵”同志）
proposed.ja: 消防隊長；ナソーソフ同志（「ポンプ」同志）

terms.gloss: A street renamed 'after Comrade Gubernsky' — a satirical Soviet renaming pun (губернский = 'provincial').
terms.why_hard: 'Gubernsky' looks like a surname but echoes 'provincial'; the joke is a street named after Comrade Provincial.

proposed.ja: グベルンスキー同志通り

terms.gloss: Car belonging to the uispolkom — the district (uyezd) executive committee of the soviet.
terms.why_hard: Soviet acronym; must be made intelligible without a footnote while keeping the officious ring.

proposed.ja: 郡執行委員会（ウイスポルコム）の車

terms.gloss: Father Fyodor's parish, the church of Saints Florus and Laurus (Frol and Lavr).
terms.why_hard: Saints' names are Russified; render with the recognizable Orthodox saints, not a phonetic 'Frol and Lavr' alone.

proposed.en: the Church of SS Florus and Laurus (Frol and Lavr)
proposed.zh: 弗罗尔和拉夫尔（圣弗洛鲁斯与劳鲁斯）教堂
proposed.ja: フロルとラヴル（聖フロルスと聖ラウルス）教会

terms.gloss: Orthodox hymn to the Theotokos, 'It Is Truly Meet'; Father Fyodor hums it when scheming.
terms.why_hard: A specific liturgical chant, not a stray phrase; the humor is a greedy priest crooning a sacred hymn.

terms.gloss: Father Fyodor's lifelong dream of owning his own candle factory in Samara.
terms.why_hard: A recurring leitmotif for the priest's greed across the book; must be rendered identically each time it returns.

terms.gloss: An 'acquisitor/money-grubber' — the theological term for grasping worldliness, applied deadpan to a priest.
terms.why_hard: Loaded church word (opposite of monastic нестяжание, non-possession); a bland 'greedy' loses the ironic sanctity.

proposed.ja: 蓄財に取り憑かれた男

terms.gloss: State-trust 'Plough-and-Hammer' brand soap, against which Father Fyodor's home-boiled soap fails.
terms.why_hard: Parody of Soviet trust brand names echoing the hammer-and-sickle; a literal render loses the trademark joke.

terms.gloss: The unnamed district town where the action opens — a Gogolian 'town of N—' convention.
terms.why_hard: Literary device (nameless 'N' town) nodding to Gogol; keep the placeholder rather than inventing a name.

conventions: Bezenchuk's death-words form a register ladder graded by the dead person's social rank (преставилась → богу душу отдать → сыграть в ящик → приказал долго жить → ноги протянул → дуба дать → гигнулся); choose target death idioms that keep the same genteel-to-crude ordering and never collapse them into one verb.

Keep clerical and social honorifics as fixed titles (отец=Father, матушка/попадья=the priest's wife, господин=Mr/Monsieur) and preserve the ты/вы asymmetry — Vorobyaninov speaks down (ты) to Bezenchuk while Bezenchuk answers up (вы + господин) — via register in en/zh and honorific level in ja.

Render Soviet acronyms and renamings (уисполком, улица товарища Губернского, 'плуг-и-молотовское') so the reader grasps them without a footnote while keeping the deadpan satire, and transliterate every personal name identically across en, zh and ja.

terms.gloss: The young con man, the novel's central schemer.
terms.why_hard: Bind one spelling book-wide; the given name is Остап, not 'Ostap' or 'Osip'.

proposed.ja: オスタップ・ベンデル

terms.gloss: Former marshal of the nobility, now hunting the chairs; addressed by name+patronymic.
terms.why_hard: Full name, patronymic and surname must stay consistent; the text alternates between all three forms.

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇·沃罗比亚尼诺夫
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ・ヴォロビヤニノフ

terms.gloss: Ostap's running epithet, roughly 'the grand schemer/operator'.
terms.why_hard: Not a job; 'great combinator' is a calque. It is a fixed epithet that recurs and must be identical each time.

terms.gloss: The two mock-grandly call their treasure hunt a business 'concession' and themselves concessionaires.
terms.why_hard: A NEP-era foreign-investment 'concession' joke; keep the deadpan business framing, not a literal 'franchise'.

proposed.zh: 特许承包人 / 承包事业
proposed.ja: 利権事業の共同経営者 / コンセッション

terms.gloss: Bezenchuk, the undertaker from Vorobyaninov's home town; recurs later.
terms.why_hard: 'гробовых дел мастер' is a mock-solemn trade title (coffin-master); render consistently as his epithet.

proposed.ja: 棺桶屋のベゼンチューク

terms.gloss: Ostap's catchphrase, literally 'the ice has broken up' — things are moving.
terms.why_hard: A recurring signature line; must land as the same memorable phrase every time it returns.

terms.gloss: Malaya Arnautskaya St. in Odessa, proverbially where all 'contraband' is really made.
terms.why_hard: The joke ('all contraband is made in Odessa') is lost without knowing the street's proverbial meaning.

proposed.zh: 敖德萨小阿尔纳乌特街
proposed.ja: オデッサのマーラヤ・アルナウツカヤ通り

terms.gloss: Dnieprostroi, the giant Dnieper hydroelectric dam then being built — a Soviet showpiece.
terms.why_hard: Ostap's dream (Taras Bulba selling its postcards) is a topical anachronistic gag needing the referent.

proposed.ja: ドニエプル発電所建設（ドニエプロストロイ）

terms.gloss: Head of Maslotrest, a state butter/fats trust.
terms.why_hard: A NEP-era compound acronym for a state trust; render transparently, not transliterate blind.

proposed.en: the manager of the Butter Trust
proposed.ja: バター・トラストの支配人

terms.gloss: Criminal Investigation Department (уголовный розыск), the police detective branch.
terms.why_hard: Clipped compound; a naive reader sees a scary word — render as the plain institution.

terms.gloss: The 2nd Home of the Social-Welfare Dept — an old-folks' almshouse, a chief setting.
terms.why_hard: соцобес is an acronym for the welfare bureau; the 'home' is a poorhouse, not a residence.

proposed.en: the 2nd Home of the Social Welfare Dept.
proposed.zh: 社会保障局第二养老院
proposed.ja: 社会保障局第二ホーム

terms.gloss: The municipal housing department that requisitioned the furniture in 1919.
terms.why_hard: Acronym-clip for 'housing department'; keep it plain and consistent, it recurs in the chair trail.

terms.gloss: 'Hero of Labour', a real Soviet honorific — here sarcastic, aimed at the drunk yardman.
terms.why_hard: The irony dies if read literally; it is a genuine state title used as a jibe.

terms.gloss: Taras Bulba, Gogol's Cossack hero; appears absurdly in Ostap's dream.
terms.why_hard: An allusion to Gogol; keep the standard literary spelling readers can look up.

terms.gloss: 'Titanic', the brand of the disastrous hair dye; also the chapter title's referent.
terms.why_hard: Not the ship as event — it is a dye brand; the chapter pun on 'traces of the Titanic' must survive.

terms.gloss: Velvet 'Tolstoy blouses' — loose belted shirts fashionable then.
terms.why_hard: толстовка is a garment named after Tolstoy, not a hoodie or a person; needs a clothing gloss.

proposed.zh: 天鹅绒托尔斯泰式衬衫
proposed.ja: ビロードのトルストイ風ブラウス

terms.gloss: Darned Jaeger woollen underwear — a bourgeois brand of the old regime.
terms.why_hard: 'егерское' is the Jaeger wool-hygiene brand, a class marker, not a hunter's outfit.

proposed.zh: 打过补丁的耶格尔羊毛内衣
proposed.ja: 繕った跡のあるイエーガー製ウール肌着

terms.gloss: A Primus, the pressurized-kerosene stove of the era; here suggested for drying hair.
terms.why_hard: A specific portable stove, not a generic 'stove'; recurs across the book's domestic scenes.

terms.gloss: 'A grave, citizen Vorobyaninov' — i.e. my lips are sealed, silent as the grave.
terms.why_hard: Literal 'grave' loses the 'you can trust my silence' idiom; keep the pledge, keep 'citizen' as address.

proposed.en: Silent as the grave, citizen Vorobyaninov.
proposed.zh: 守口如瓶，沃罗比亚尼诺夫公民。
proposed.ja: 墓場まで持っていきます、ヴォロビヤニノフ公民。

terms.gloss: 'like a soldier at a louse' — a look of cold, murderous loathing.
terms.why_hard: A vivid fixed simile; render it as an image of contempt, not word-for-word if it reads flat.

proposed.en: like a soldier eyeing a louse
proposed.ja: シラミを見る兵隊のような目つきで

conventions: Ostap's running epithets (великий комбинатор; директор-учредитель концессии; главный руководитель работ и технический директор) are fixed labels: render each identically at every recurrence, keeping the mock-solemn bureaucratic deadpan.

NEP compound-acronym institutions (жилотдел, соцобес, угрозыск, Маслотрест, Днепрострой) get a plain, transparent target-language rendering in line; reserve a translator's note only for those whose joke depends on the acronym (Малая Арнаутская, герой труда).

Preserve the ты/вы split — Ostap uses вы to Vorobyaninov but ты to servants and the yardman; carry the shift into Japanese honorific register and mark it in English/Chinese where the change of footing matters.

terms.gloss: Stargorod's meddling jack-of-all-trades locksmith-mechanic.
terms.why_hard: Given-name+patronymic and surname 'Polesov' must map to one person.

proposed.zh: 维克托·米哈伊洛维奇·波列索夫
proposed.ja: ヴィクトル・ミハイロヴィチ・ポレソフ

terms.gloss: The honest chief engineer who built the Stargorod tramway.
terms.why_hard: Fix one spelling; don't gloss the comic name (треух = earflap cap).

terms.gloss: The tramway-trust boss who chairs the opening rally.
terms.why_hard: One spelling; his malapropisms mark the speech, keep the name plain.

terms.gloss: A visiting journalist's comic byline; puns 'flywheel' against Hamlet, Prince of Denmark.
terms.why_hard: A literal 'Prince Flywheel / Flywheel the Dane' loses both the Hamlet joke and the machine pun.

proposed.ja: プリンス・フライホイール(デンマークのフライホイール)

terms.gloss: Fictional provincial town, main setting of Part One.
terms.why_hard: Fixed transliteration; not 'Old Town' though star- hints at 'old'.

terms.gloss: Vorobyaninov's abolished tsarist rank, 'marshal of the nobility', now his epithet.
terms.why_hard: 'Leader/chief' misses the defunct pre-revolutionary office it must read as.

terms.gloss: Soviet central dairy/butter marketing trust (the Butter Centre).
terms.why_hard: An acronymic NEP trust; a literal 'Oil Center' reads as petroleum.

proposed.zh: 马斯洛岑特尔(黄油托拉斯)
proposed.ja: マスロツェントル(バター公社)

terms.gloss: Provincial (gubernia) executive committee of soviets; its chairman opens the line.
terms.why_hard: Soviet administrative acronym; don't invent a modern council name.

terms.gloss: Unpaid volunteer-labor 'Saturdays' worked for the state.
terms.why_hard: Not just 'Saturdays'; the ideological volunteer-work sense must survive.

proposed.ja: スボートニク(義務労働の土曜日)

terms.gloss: Trade union (and its club) of municipal/utilities workers.
terms.why_hard: 'Communal' reads as 'communist'; it means public-utilities staff.

terms.gloss: 'The international situation' — the empty oratorical set-piece every speaker slides into.
terms.why_hard: Must be rendered identically at each recurrence or the repeated-joke structure collapses.

terms.term: Трамвай построить — это не ешака купить
terms.gloss: Gavrilin's folksy aphorism: building a tram is no trifle (lit. not like buying a donkey).
terms.why_hard: 'ешак' is southern dialect for donkey; keep the homely-proverb feel, not standard 'осёл'.

proposed.en: Building a tram's not like buying a donkey
proposed.zh: 修有轨电车可不比买头毛驴
proposed.ja: 路面電車を造るのはロバを買うのとはわけが違う

terms.term: не за страх, а за совесть
terms.gloss: To work 'not from fear but from conscience' — sincerely, wholeheartedly.
terms.why_hard: A set Soviet phrase; a clumsy literal fear-vs-conscience gloss kills the rhythm.

proposed.en: not out of fear but out of conscience
proposed.zh: 不是出于畏惧,而是出于良心
proposed.ja: 恐れからではなく良心から

terms.term: акробаты пера, виртуозы фарса, шакалы ротационных машин
terms.gloss: A French communist's tirade against the bourgeois press: acrobats of the pen, virtuosos of farce, jackals of the rotary presses.
terms.why_hard: Keep the three rising parallel epithets; 'ротационные машины' are printing presses, not machines in general.

proposed.en: acrobats of the pen, virtuosos of farce, jackals of the rotary presses
proposed.zh: 笔杆子的杂技演员、闹剧的名家、轮转印刷机的豺狼
proposed.ja: ペンの曲芸師、笑劇の名手、輪転機のジャッカル

terms.gloss: British foreign secretary Austen Chamberlain, stock 1920s Soviet propaganda villain.
terms.why_hard: Not Neville; the 1927 anti-Soviet rupture makes this Austen — the reader needs the right man.

proposed.ja: (オースティン・)チェンバレン

terms.gloss: U.S. Senator William Borah, isolationist, prominent in the era's Soviet press.
terms.why_hard: 'Bora' must be restored to 'Borah'; the reader won't recognize the bare transliteration.

terms.gloss: 'The Romanian boyars' — Soviet epithet for Romania's rulers amid the Bessarabia dispute.
terms.why_hard: 'Boyars' for a 20th-century state is deliberate propaganda scorn, not medieval nobles.

proposed.zh: 罗马尼亚的波雅尔(大贵族)
proposed.ja: ルーマニアのボヤール(大貴族)

terms.gloss: The march honoring Red cavalry commander Semyon Budyonny.
terms.why_hard: The name Budyonny must stay recognizable; it's a specific Civil-War song.

proposed.ja: ブジョーンヌイ行進曲

terms.gloss: A short brass fanfare flourish played at ceremonies (Tusch).
terms.why_hard: Not 'a touch'; it's a specific ceremonial musical salute, easily mistranslated.

proposed.ja: 祝典のファンファーレ(トゥッシュ)

conventions: Transliterate every personal name and keep the given-name+patronymic form; bind one spelling per character (Vorobyaninov/'Kisa', Polesov = Viktor Mikhailovich) so one person is never split across renderings.
Render the running set-pieces — 'международное положение' and the newspaper clichés set in guillemets — identically at each recurrence, so the deadpan repetition reads as the joke it is.

Carry Soviet/NEP acronym-institutions (Маслоцентр, губисполком, союз коммунальников) as a transliteration plus a short in-text gloss on first use, reserving translator's notes for what no gloss can carry.

terms.gloss: The narrator's signature recurring epithet for Ostap; a virtuoso schemer/operator.
terms.why_hard: 'Комбинатор' isn't 'combiner'; it means a wheeler-dealer. Must be one fixed epithet used every time.

terms.gloss: Mock-title for the two treasure hunters, framing their scheme as a business 'concession'.
terms.why_hard: It's an ironic NEP-era commercial metaphor, not a literal legal role; the joke recurs book-wide.

terms.gloss: The yardman's/janitor's lodge where the pair first camp out.
terms.why_hard: A specific pre/post-revolutionary domestic space, not a generic 'room'; ties to the дворник figure Tikhon.

terms.gloss: Member of the Union of Soviet Trade Employees, per the forged union card.
terms.why_hard: 'совторгслужащих' is a stacked Soviet acronym-compound; the comedy is its bureaucratic mouthful.

proposed.en: member of the Union of Soviet Trade Employees
proposed.zh: 苏维埃商业职员工会会员
proposed.ja: ソビエト商業職員組合員

terms.gloss: Trade-union membership booklet, the forged ID Ostap hands over.
terms.why_hard: A specific Soviet document, not a generic 'card'; carries the identity gag.

terms.gloss: Non-Party (not a member of the Communist Party), a routine census/ID category.
terms.why_hard: Loaded Soviet status term; 'independent/nonpartisan' misreads it.

terms.gloss: The seedy 'Sorbonne' furnished-rooms hotel where they lodge.
terms.why_hard: Pretentious European name on a flophouse is the joke; keep the name, mark the register.

terms.gloss: Stargorod communal-services administration holding the housing archive.
terms.why_hard: Contracted Soviet agency name (Star-gorod + kommunalnoe khozyaystvo); transliterating the acronym loses sense.

proposed.zh: 斯塔尔戈罗德市政公用事业局
proposed.ja: スタルゴロド市営公共事業局

terms.gloss: The Housing Department, disbanded 1921, whose archive holds the chair-distribution orders.
terms.why_hard: Another Soviet acronym-office; render as a transparent department name, consistently.

terms.gloss: Chancellery of the pre-revolutionary city governor's office, where Korobeinikov once served.
terms.why_hard: Tsarist-era institution; градоначальник is a city governor, not a mayor. Marks the old regime.

terms.gloss: Euphemistic NEP job-label ('worker of office labour') for a clerk.
terms.why_hard: Deliberately inflated bureaucratic phrasing; flattening to 'clerk' kills the parody.

terms.gloss: The archivist who sells copies of the furniture-distribution orders.
terms.why_hard: Fixed transliteration; surname echoes 'peddler' (коробейник) — a quiet characterization.

proposed.zh: 瓦尔福洛梅·科罗别伊尼科夫
proposed.ja: ヴァルフォロメイ・コロベイニコフ

terms.gloss: Archivist (mock-grand title for Korobeinikov), keeper of the records.
terms.why_hard: Slightly archaic/pompous register vs plain 'archivist'; the narrator uses it for comic weight.

terms.gloss: Marshal of the nobility, Vorobyaninov's former rank ('предводитель').
terms.why_hard: Specific tsarist elective office; 'leader of the nobility' is wrong — it's a fixed historical title.

terms.gloss: Morganatic (unequal-rank) marriage, invoked by Ostap to explain his 'noble' bastardy.
terms.why_hard: Precise dynastic-law term; the humor is Ostap deploying aristocratic jargon con-artistically.

terms.gloss: 'Don't be a ladybird' = don't be a meek, naive simpleton.
terms.why_hard: Literal 'ladybird/God's cow' means nothing to the target reader; render the sense, not the bug.

terms.gloss: Proverb 'you can't spoil kasha with butter'; puns with 'каша заваривалась' (a mess was brewing).
terms.why_hard: The two porridge phrases must be rendered so the pun/echo survives, not each in isolation.

proposed.en: you can't spoil porridge with butter
proposed.ja: バターで粥は不味くならぬ

terms.gloss: An innocent children's game of 'rat', to which Ostap likens their petty forgery.
terms.why_hard: A period children's game; keep the harmless-play image without inventing a specific rule.

terms.gloss: Absurd sample aliases — a Greek-Odessa name and a 'stink'-rooted surname — Ostap says are worse than Michelson.
terms.why_hard: Зловунов is a coined comic name (from 'зловоние', stench); it should read as funny, not neutral.

proposed.zh: 什么帕帕-赫里斯托佐普洛或臭烘诺夫
proposed.ja: パパ・フリストゾプロだのクサヴノフだの

terms.gloss: A railway-workers' outskirt district of Stargorod where Korobeinikov lives.
terms.why_hard: Invented place-name with an augmentative 'goose' ring; transliterate, keep consistent.

conventions: Render every 1920s Soviet acronym-office (Старкомхоз, жилотдел, союз совторгслужащих) by a transparent descriptive department name in each language rather than transliterating the acronym, so the bureaucratic joke lands without a footnote.
Fix one transliteration per name per language on first use (Ostap Bender = 奥斯塔普·本德尔 = オスタップ・ベンデル); give the patronymic on first mention, then drop it.

Preserve the narrator's mock-solemn deadpan: keep legal/bureaucratic register verbatim (e.g. 'предусмотренное Уголовным кодексом', 'работник конторского труда') and mark servile speech tics like the '-с' suffix ('Почему-с?') as deference, never flattened to plain speech.

terms.gloss: Viktor Mikhailovich Polesov, the meddling mechanic with a motorcycle.
terms.why_hard: Recurring minor character; keep spelling stable and don't confuse patronymic with surname.

terms.gloss: Elena Stanislavovna, the fortune-teller hosting the conspirators' meeting.
terms.why_hard: Name only, no surname on these pages; keep patronymic form consistent.

proposed.zh: 叶莲娜·斯坦尼斯拉沃夫娜
proposed.ja: エレーナ・スタニスラーヴォヴナ

terms.gloss: Kislyarsky, a nervous NEP private trader terrified into 'donating'.
terms.why_hard: Recurring; the -ский ending needs a consistent zh/ja spelling.

terms.gloss: 'giant of thought' — Ostap's mock-grand epithet for the dim Vorobyaninov.
terms.why_hard: A running gag repeated across the book; must be rendered identically each time, kept deadpan not literal-clunky.

terms.gloss: 'father of Russian democracy' — Ostap's absurd honorific for Vorobyaninov.
terms.why_hard: Recurring epithet, ironic; the joke dies if it varies between recurrences.

terms.gloss: 'a personage close to the Emperor' — the pompous third epithet for Vorobyaninov.
terms.why_hard: Chancery/court register; императору means the tsar, not any generic emperor.

proposed.en: a personage close to the Emperor

terms.gloss: 'the grand strategist' — the narrator's standing epithet for Ostap the schemer.
terms.why_hard: комбинатор = wheeler-dealer/schemer, not 'combinator'; iconic phrase with a canonical rendering to match.

terms.gloss: 'Union of Sword and Ploughshare' — the fake monarchist conspiracy Ostap invents to extort money.
terms.why_hard: орало is archaic/biblical (Isaiah 'swords into ploughshares', here inverted); parodies White-émigré fronts; it is the chapter title.

proposed.en: the Union of Sword and Ploughshare

terms.gloss: 'Bystro-upak' (QuickPack), Dyadyev's NEP packaging firm; its owner is a target of the scam.
terms.why_hard: Invented Soviet-style compressed trade name (bystro+upakovka); should read as a NEP business coinage, not a surname.

proposed.ja: ブィストロウパーク（速包社）

terms.gloss: Besprizorniki — the mass of orphaned homeless children of the civil-war/NEP years.
terms.why_hard: A specific Soviet social phenomenon; 'homeless children' undersells it, but a footnote-free rendering is needed.

terms.gloss: 'flowers on the asphalt' — Ostap's mock-lyrical figure for the street waifs (vs. 'цветы улицы').
terms.why_hard: Pairs with 'цветы жизни'; keep the flower imagery linked across all three phrases.

terms.gloss: 'children are the flowers of life' — a sentimental proverb (via Gorky) Ostap wields cynically.
terms.why_hard: A recognizable Russian cliché; render as a set proverb, keeping the 'flower' link to his other lines.

proposed.en: children are the flowers of life

terms.gloss: A nobleman of the pre-revolutionary hereditary gentry — a dangerous class label by 1928.
terms.why_hard: Not merely 'noble/gentleman'; carries the loaded pre-rev estate meaning central to the interrogation joke.

terms.gloss: The Imperial Guards regiments — Ostap's 'which regiment did you serve in?' assumes tsarist officer pedigree.
terms.why_hard: 'Guards' as elite tsarist units, not any modern guard; the class marker drives the running interrogation gag.

terms.gloss: 'The West will help us' (also 'Запад нам поможет') — Ostap's proverbial con-man promise of foreign aid.
terms.why_hard: Became a Russian catchphrase; keep both variants consistent so the running promise reads as one refrain.

proposed.ja: 外国が我々を助けてくれる

terms.gloss: 'Bear up / take heart' — Ostap's mock-conspiratorial exhortation, repeated to each mark.
terms.why_hard: Recurring one-word refrain; must stay the same solemn-comic phrase every time, not paraphrased.

terms.gloss: 'gentlemen of the jury' — Ostap's courtroom-oratory tag dropped absurdly into a fundraising speech.
terms.why_hard: A fixed legal-address cliché he parodies; render as the set courtroom phrase to land the incongruity.

terms.gloss: 'private capital' — NEP-era private business; Kislyarsky is addressed as its representative (a nepman).
terms.why_hard: Loaded 1920s economic term for the tolerated-but-suspect private trader; not generic 'capital'.

terms.gloss: The NEP 'equalization levy' (уравнительный сбор) on private traders, which the merchants grumble about.
terms.why_hard: Elliptical NEP tax term; a translator who misses the dropped 'сбор' won't know it names a specific tax.

terms.gloss: 'a one-man hussar with a motor' — Ostap's mock-heroic title for Polesov on his motorcycle.
terms.why_hard: Puns on 'извозчик-одиночка' (a lone cabby) crossed with 'hussar'; keep the absurd swagger, not literal jargon.

proposed.en: a one-man hussar with a motor
proposed.ja: 一匹狼のモーター付き軽騎兵

conventions: Transliterate all personal names consistently and follow standard published renderings for Ostap Bender and Vorobyaninov; give full patronymic on first mention, short form thereafter.

Render the running epithets (гигант мысли, отец русской демократии, особа приближенная к императору, великий комбинатор) word-for-word identically at every recurrence — they are book-wide running gags.
вы is the default polite address; keep Ostap's mock-solemn bureaucratic/legal register deadpan-formal rather than colloquial, and in Japanese use plain-formal, not heaped keigo.

terms.gloss: The protagonist: a former marshal of the nobility, now a registry-office clerk
terms.why_hard: Name+patronymic must stay fixed and be the default reference throughout; do not collapse to a bare first name

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ

terms.gloss: Ippolit Matveyevich's surname; sometimes used alone by the narrator
terms.why_hard: Must match the surname used everywhere else in the book; keep one transliteration

terms.gloss: Ippolit Matveyevich's dying mother-in-law, madame Petukhova
terms.why_hard: The chapter title calls her 'мадам Петухова'; keep first-name form and surname form consistent and linked

proposed.zh: 克拉芙季娅·伊万诺芙娜
proposed.ja: クラウディヤ・イワーノヴナ

terms.gloss: The drunken coffin-maker who recurs through the early chapters
terms.why_hard: Recurring comic character; fix the transliteration once

terms.gloss: Bezenchuk's garbled rustic swear-tag, roughly 'blast the thing'
terms.why_hard: A nonsense oath that is a running gag; must be rendered identically every time, not paraphrased freshly

terms.gloss: A rival undertaker's firm that Bezenchuk resents
terms.why_hard: It is a business name (the Nymph), not a mythological reference; keep quoted and consistent

terms.gloss: Old-fashioned trade title, 'master of the coffin trade' = undertaker
terms.why_hard: The archaic solemn phrasing is part of the joke; don't flatten to plain 'undertaker' everywhere

terms.gloss: Clerk at ZAGS, the Soviet civil registry of births, marriages and deaths
terms.why_hard: ZAGS is a specific Soviet institution; 'clerk' loses the bureaucratic bathos of a former aristocrat filing marriages

terms.gloss: Workplace mutual-aid fund that gave staff small advances
terms.why_hard: A NEP-era workplace institution, not a bank; 'advance from the mutual-aid fund' must read as routine petty bureaucracy

terms.gloss: The fictional provincial town where the story opens
terms.why_hard: Invented place name (echoes 'old town'); keep one transliteration across the book

terms.gloss: Furniture by Hambs, a famous St Petersburg cabinetmaking firm — a mark of quality
terms.why_hard: Not a random adjective: it signals the chairs are valuable heirloom pieces, the whole plot's MacGuffin

terms.gloss: A matched drawing-room suite: sofa, twelve chairs and a round table
terms.why_hard: The 'twelve chairs' of the title come from this suite; render the set consistently so the count and title line up

terms.gloss: The diamonds sewn into a chair seat — the object of the whole chase
terms.why_hard: Central plot MacGuffin; keep one word (not variously gems/jewels/brilliants) throughout the book

terms.gloss: Pre-revolutionary honorific 'Mr/sir' Bezenchuk uses, jarring in Soviet 1927
terms.why_hard: The obsolete address is deliberate class comedy; 'comrade' or a neutral 'Mr' erases the anachronistic deference

proposed.ja: ヴォロビヤニノフの旦那

terms.gloss: Soviet 'militia' police, contrasted with the Tsarist 'polizia' of 1897
terms.why_hard: The text deliberately pairs old police and new militia; collapsing both to 'police' loses the before/after-revolution joke

terms.gloss: The mock-French salon nickname of the town barber
terms.why_hard: A provincial's pretentious French branding; keep the French flavour, don't translate the names into the target language

proposed.ja: 「ピエールとコンスタンタン」

terms.gloss: A small bust of Vasily Zhukovsky, the Romantic poet, in the town square
terms.why_hard: Reader must know he is a revered classic poet for the graffiti gag to land; may need a light note

proposed.ja: 詩人ジュコフスキーの胸像

terms.gloss: 'Hemoglobin' — the barber's mock-scientific patter, 'the whole secret is in the hemoglobin'
terms.why_hard: Comic pseudo-science; keep the clinical word so the deadpan pomposity survives

terms.gloss: Ippolit Matveyevich's pince-nez, a recurring visual attribute
terms.why_hard: A signature object that keeps appearing; use one consistent term

terms.gloss: A peaked cloth workman's cap, here Bezenchuk's
terms.why_hard: Class-marked headgear (a worker's cap, not a hat); don't render as generic 'hat'

terms.gloss: 'Tango Amapa', a popular tango tune of the 1910s-20s
terms.why_hard: A real period song evoking cheap glamour; keep the title, italicised, not translated literally

terms.gloss: The agronomist's wife (colloquial feminine of 'agronomist')
terms.why_hard: The -ша suffix marks her only as the wife-of; keep that relational, slightly folksy tone

conventions: Names: transliterate once and reuse; give full first-name + patronymic on first mention, then default to 'Ippolit Matveyevich'; carry patronymics into zh and ja rather than dropping them.
Keep the вы/ты register: the dying mother-in-law and Ippolit address each other with formal вы — render as formal/polite throughout (in ja via です/ます and 敬語 for the older speaker).
Render dialogue with the target language's own convention (em-dash in en, 破折号/引号 in zh, 「」in ja), but keep Bezenchuk's recurring tag «туды ее в качель» worded identically on every appearance.

terms.gloss: Ostap Bender, the young con man and 'chief concessionaire' of the treasure hunt.
terms.why_hard: Given here only by first name; must map to the same character rendered elsewhere as Бендер, not a new person.

terms.gloss: Varfolomei Korobeinikov, the archivist who sells stolen furniture requisition orders.
terms.why_hard: Appears as surname, first name Варфоломей, and the familiar Варфоломеич — all one man, not three.

terms.gloss: Familiar/patronymic-only form of Korobeinikov as the locals address him.
terms.why_hard: Not a separate character; the affectionate-rustic tone of the short form must survive.

terms.gloss: Father Fyodor Vostrikov, the priest secretly hunting the same chairs.
terms.why_hard: 'отец' is the clerical honorific 'Father', not the word 'father'; surname Востриков is the same man.

terms.gloss: Ippolit Vorobyaninov, ex-marshal of the nobility, whose family furniture is sought.
terms.why_hard: Long surname needs one fixed transliteration; the -ья- cluster is easily mangled.

terms.gloss: The real St Petersburg furniture maker Gambs; 'a Gambs piece' signalled quality.
terms.why_hard: A brand, not a common word; the whole plot turns on the Gambs chairs, so it must stay recognisable.

proposed.zh: 冈布斯出品／冈布斯家具厂
proposed.ja: ガンブス製／ガンブス工房

terms.gloss: The drawing-room suite of the widow/wife of General Popov, indexed under П.
terms.why_hard: 'генеральша' = a general's wife/widow, not a female general; a title, not a name.

proposed.zh: 波波娃将军夫人的家具
proposed.ja: ポポワ将軍夫人の家具一式

terms.gloss: Archivist/registrar; Korobeinikov's petty-clerk office, comically grand.
terms.why_hard: The archaic Latinate word carries mock-solemnity that flat 'clerk' loses.

terms.gloss: Pre-revolutionary rank 'head of chancellery'; Ostap uses it to flatter the clerk.
terms.why_hard: An obsolete Imperial bureaucratic rank deployed ironically; not a modern job title.

terms.gloss: Ostap's self-styled epithet 'chief concessionaire' of the chair-hunting 'concession'.
terms.why_hard: The running joke frames the scheme as a business concession; must stay consistent everywhere.

proposed.ja: 筆頭コンセッション業者

terms.gloss: 'fighter for the cause/idea' — Ostap's mock-honorific for the greedy clerk.
terms.why_hard: Heavily ironic Soviet cliché; a literal earnest rendering kills the sarcasm.

proposed.ja: 理想のために闘う戦士

terms.gloss: 'The ice has broken, gentlemen of the jury!' — Ostap's signature catch-phrase, now a Russian proverb.
terms.why_hard: Famous quotation recurring across the book; must be word-for-word identical everywhere and echo the courtroom flourish.

proposed.en: The ice has broken, gentlemen of the jury!
proposed.zh: 坚冰已经打破，陪审员先生们！
proposed.ja: 氷は動き出した、陪審員の諸君！

terms.gloss: Coaxing term of endearment, lit. 'little dove', used mock-tenderly.
terms.why_hard: Not a name; the false warmth toward a man he is cheating must come through.

terms.gloss: Breezy command 'Go ahead!/Fire away!' urging the clerk to write.
terms.why_hard: 1920s colloquial imperative unrelated to its literal 'cut/cover' senses.

terms.gloss: Mock farewell 'Write me letters!', a jeering brush-off as Ostap leaves.
terms.why_hard: A recurring taunting sign-off; literal politeness misses the derision.

terms.gloss: 'cannibal interest rates' — Korobeinikov's usurious pawnbroking terms.
terms.why_hard: The vivid 'cannibal' image should be kept, not flattened to 'exorbitant'.

proposed.ja: 人を食ったような高利

terms.gloss: 'I'm telling you in plain Russian' — set phrase for exasperated emphasis.
terms.why_hard: Idiomatic; a literal 'in the Russian language' reads as nonsense.

proposed.en: I'm telling you in plain Russian
proposed.ja: はっきり言ってやってるだろう

terms.gloss: Soviet requisition/allocation orders assigning confiscated furniture to recipients.
terms.why_hard: NEP-era paperwork, not 'orders' in the commercial or military sense; the plot's MacGuffin.

terms.gloss: Pre-revolutionary ten-ruble gold coins; желтяки is slang 'yellow-boys'.
terms.why_hard: Period currency traded by rate against chervontsy; not modern rubles, and the slang term is easily lost.

proposed.ja: 十ルーブル金貨／黄金貨

terms.term: пепельница ... на манер калоши с красной надписью «Треугольник»
terms.gloss: Ashtray shaped like a galosh marked 'Treugolnik', the Leningrad rubber trust's brand.
terms.why_hard: 'Triangle' is a real Soviet galosh brand; the joke needs the reader to see cheap promotional kitsch.

proposed.ja: 「トレウゴーリニク（三角）」印のゴム長靴型灰皿

terms.gloss: 'The Shepherdess', a mass-produced pastoral tapestry Korobeinikov prizes.
terms.why_hard: 'гобелен' is a woven wall-tapestry, not embroidery; the title should read as sentimental kitsch.

proposed.ja: 「羊飼いの娘」のタペストリー

terms.gloss: 'The alphabet, mirror of life' — Korobeinikov's card index and the chapter's title.
terms.why_hard: Doubles as the chapter heading; the grandiose slogan must match the title rendering exactly.

proposed.en: the alphabet, that mirror of life
proposed.ja: アルファベット——生活の鏡

terms.gloss: The town district nicknamed Gusishche where Korobeinikov lives.
terms.why_hard: A local toponym, not a common noun; keep it as a place name.

conventions: Transliterate every personal name once by a single consistent system, and render short/patronymic-only forms (Варфоломеич) as the same character's familiar name, never a new person; keep Ostap's clerical/rank honorifics (отец, правитель канцелярии) as honorifics.

Preserve Ostap's mock-solemn register: reproduce his recurring catch-phrases ('Лед тронулся, господа присяжные заседатели!', 'Пишите письма!') verbatim and identically every time they recur, since they are the book's running jokes.

Mark the ты/вы drop when Ostap turns contemptuous ('Тише, дурак', 'говорят тебе') — in Japanese via plain/rude forms, in Chinese and English via diction — and keep the Russian em-dash dialogue style with one consistent per-language marker.

terms.gloss: The young con man protagonist; charming, quick-witted 'grand strategist'.
terms.why_hard: Central recurring name; transliteration must be fixed once and match the title epithet Великий комбинатор used of him.

proposed.ja: オスタップ・ベンデル

terms.gloss: The fictional provincial town where the chair hunt begins.
terms.why_hard: Invented name ('Old-town'); pick transliteration or gloss and keep it, since Стар- prefixes many local institutions.

terms.gloss: A homeless, parentless street child of the post-Civil-War era.
terms.why_hard: Not a generic 'beggar boy'; it names a specific mass social phenomenon of the 1920s.

terms.gloss: An astrolabe, the surveying instrument Bender hawks and sells as junk.
terms.why_hard: Recurring comic prop; 'Сама меряет' joke rides on it being a real, absurdly useless instrument.

terms.gloss: Zhenotdel: the Communist Party women's department.
terms.why_hard: A real Party organ, not 'women's shops'; the discount joke needs the reader to feel it as officialdom.

terms.gloss: Stargorod provincial criminal-investigation department (a Soviet acronym-name).
terms.why_hard: Portmanteau (Star-gub-rozysk); comedy is in the bureaucratic compression, so keep the mock-official feel.

proposed.zh: 斯塔尔哥罗德省刑侦局
proposed.ja: スタルゴロド県刑事捜査局

terms.gloss: Maslotsentr: the state butter/dairy marketing trust.
terms.why_hard: A real NEP-era trust; the stolen-typewriter aside only lands if it reads as a dull agency.

proposed.zh: 黄油托拉斯（马斯洛采恩特尔）
proposed.ja: バター公団（マスロツェントル）

terms.gloss: Marshal of the nobility, the elected pre-revolutionary district gentry official.
terms.why_hard: Vorobyaninov's former rank and a running theme; 'buржуй/пролетарий' gag depends on getting this exact estate title right.

terms.gloss: 'A Turkish subject' — Bender's stock line about his father, a comic badge of shady exotic origin.
terms.why_hard: Recurring catchphrase ('сын турецко-подданного'); must be worded identically each time to keep the running joke.

terms.gloss: Street of the Lena Events, named for the 1912 Lena goldfields massacre of striking miners.
terms.why_hard: 'события' is not generic 'events'; it points to a specific pre-revolutionary atrocity used in Soviet street-renaming.

terms.gloss: Bender's imagined painting, a Soviet parody title spun off Repin's Cossacks canvas.
terms.why_hard: The joke is the parody echo; its wording must visibly mirror the Repin title rendered below.

proposed.en: The Bolsheviks Writing a Letter to Chamberlain
proposed.ja: 「ボリシェヴィキ、チェンバレンに手紙を書く」

terms.gloss: Austen Chamberlain, British Foreign Secretary and the era's stock image of the hostile West.
terms.why_hard: Reader must place him as the 1920s Soviet propaganda bogeyman, not later PM Neville Chamberlain.

terms.gloss: Repin's famous painting 'Reply of the Zaporozhian Cossacks to the Sultan'.
terms.why_hard: A real, widely-known artwork; use its established museum title so the parody above is recognisable.

proposed.en: The Zaporozhian Cossacks Writing a Letter to the Turkish Sultan
proposed.ja: 「トルコのスルタンに手紙を書くザポロージェのコサック」

terms.gloss: AKhRR, the Association of Artists of Revolutionary Russia, and its exhibition.
terms.why_hard: A real 1920s art body; the acronym must be glossed once so the satire of official art reads.

proposed.en: the AKhRR exhibition (Association of Artists of Revolutionary Russia)
proposed.zh: 革命俄罗斯美术家协会（阿赫尔）画展
proposed.ja: 革命ロシア美術家協会（アフルル）展

terms.gloss: Comrade Mikhail Kalinin, formal Soviet head of state ('all-Union elder').
terms.why_hard: 'т.' = товарищ must render as Comrade; reader must know this is a top leader for the papakha gag to bite.

terms.gloss: Comrade Georgy Chicherin, People's Commissar for Foreign Affairs.
terms.why_hard: A bespectacled diplomat; 'голым по пояс' is funny only if the reader knows how staid he was.

terms.gloss: A papakha, the tall Caucasian sheepskin/wool hat.
terms.why_hard: Not a generic fur cap; paired with the burka it evokes Cossack/Caucasus dress incongruous on Kalinin.

terms.gloss: A burka, the long felt Caucasian cloak, here white.
terms.why_hard: False friend for English 'burqa'; it is a shepherd's/warrior's cloak, the visual half of the Cossack costume joke.

proposed.ja: 白いブルカ（フェルトの外套）

terms.gloss: The dworник's comic euphemism for 'before the revolution / in the old days'.
terms.why_hard: Deadpan malapropism turning a Marxist term into a date; keep it literal so the absurdity survives.

terms.gloss: A dapple-grey suit, Bender's fantasy of the outfit a bigamist needs.
terms.why_hard: 'в яблоках' is the horse-coat term 'dappled', not literal apples; recurring image of aspirational elegance.

proposed.ja: 灰色のぶち模様の背広

terms.gloss: 'The wife on duty' — Bender's cynical term for the current wife in his bigamy scheme.
terms.why_hard: Bureaucratic 'on duty' applied to a wife is the joke; keep the office register.

terms.gloss: 'Provincial Marguerites' — small-town marriageable women, via Goethe's Faust heroine.
terms.why_hard: Literary allusion to Gretchen/Marguerite; a plain 'girls' loses the mock-romantic irony.

proposed.ja: 地方のマルガリータたち

terms.gloss: The building's yardman/caretaker (here Tikhon), lives in the basement dворницкая.
terms.why_hard: More than 'janitor': a live-in gatekeeper of pre- and post-revolutionary Russian life; recurring character.

conventions: Renamed streets: render as 'New Name (formerly Old Name)', e.g. Red Army Street (formerly Bolshaya Pushkinskaya), matching Красноармейская (бывшая Большая Пушкинская).

Soviet acronym-institutions (Старгуброзыск, Маслоцентр, Стардеткомиссия, женотдел) get a fixed transliteration plus a one-time glossed English compound; keep the mock-bureaucratic tone that carries the satire.
Bender addresses the old man with condescending ты and mock-kin terms (дядя, отец, дедушка, дед); render the false intimacy consistently rather than flattening to neutral 'sir/grandpa'.

conventions: Fix each of Ostap's recurring catchphrases (Лед тронулся…; Заседание продолжается; ключ от квартиры…) in one exact wording and repeat it verbatim at every occurrence so the running gags land.

Transliterate personal names consistently and preserve the patronymic system: full name at first mention, patronymic-only address kept as-is; ja in middle-dot katakana, zh via standard sound-transliteration.

Ostap and Ippolit address each other with formal вы; render the politeness level consistently (esp. Japanese keigo) and keep the Russian em-dash dialogue turns as a stable dialogue style in each language.

conventions: Transliterate every proper name once (Bender, Vorobyaninov, Treukhov...) and always give the same character the same forms, including name+patronymic; in ja use katakana with a middle dot and no honorific suffix on Russian names.

Keep the em-dash dialogue convention of the original as run-in dashes in en, and the running gags ('Дышите глубже...', 'концессионеры') worded identically on every recurrence.

conventions: Keep the narrator's deadpan mock-solemn voice: render its ironic officialese and lyrical parody straight, without smoothing the joke.

Transliterate personal names and give the full name-plus-patronymic on first mention, then unify every later short form to the same spelling.

conventions: Render Soviet acronyms and abbreviations (Старсобес, собес, завхоз) by their meaning, gloss the transliteration once on first use, then use one fixed short form book-wide; keep the deadpan bureaucratic register.
Preserve the mock-solemn, dry narratorial voice; never 'explain' a joke inline — use a short translator's note only where no rendering can carry the reference.
Keep parody slogans and official notices in quotation marks and in a pompous agitprop register across en/zh/ja.
